title: Stop abort being the one destructive action with no gate, and give a blocked role somewhere to go

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 694ee19 on main; working tree clean apart from .vscode/settings.json. Sprint file read fresh.

Reqs 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are met and I demonstrated each rather than reading them. Req 4 is met on the path you tested and broken on the one you didn't, in a way that loses the exact thing this sprint exists to preserve.

================================================================
BLOCKER — /sprint-block ON A SPRINT THAT WAS NEVER STARTED
HALF-COMPLETES, THEN DISCARDS THE ANALYSIS.
scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py, cmd_block: `state = load_state(args.id)`
================================================================

Reproduced end to end in a scratch repo. Create a sprint, don't start it, block it:

  before:  registry status: todo | docs/sprints/1-todo/sprint-1_never-started-sprint.md

  $ python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py block 1 --reason "the content this sprint needs does not exist yet"
  ERROR: No state file for sprint 1 in <root> (branch: main). Run /sprint-start 1 first.
  EXIT=1

  after:   registry status: blocked | docs/sprints/4-blocked/sprint-1_never-started-sprint.md
           4-blocked/: sprint-1_never-started-sprint.md
           state/: (empty)

The command reports failure and has already done most of the work: the file moved to 4-blocked, the frontmatter rewritten, the registry flipped to blocked, save_registry committed. Then load_state raises and the function dies before log_event ever runs.

WHAT THAT COSTS IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE SPRINT. Req 4 requires "the role's own stated analysis is recorded in history," and your own Context says it plainly: "What was actually lost was the analysis." On this path the analysis exists nowhere but the terminal that produced it — the sprint is sitting in 4-blocked marked blocked, with no record of why, which is strictly worse than the abandon-with-a-reason it replaces. And the error tells the reader to run /sprint-start, which would move the file straight back out and leave the analysis just as gone.

THE SIBLING COMMAND IN THE SAME FILE ALREADY HANDLES THIS. cmd_abort wraps its state write in `if state_path(args.id).exists():`. cmd_block took cmd_abort's structure — same lock pair, same registry lookup, same actor derivation, same move-and-update-frontmatter — and dropped that one guard.

DO NOT FIX IT BY COPYING THAT GUARD. Wrapping the write in `if state_path(...).exists()` makes the exit code 0 and still throws the analysis away, which passes a test and fails Req 4. For abort that guard is fine, because an abandoned sprint has nothing to preserve. For block, "succeeded but recorded no analysis" is the defect.

The fix that matches this sprint's own discipline is Req 2's ordering, applied here: validate before mutating. Check for the state file up front, alongside the --reason check, and refuse cleanly with nothing moved — something like "sprint N was never started, so there is no record to attach your analysis to; report it to Master Controller directly, or /sprint-start it first." Whatever the wording, the invariant to hold is: whenever /sprint-block reports success, the analysis is in the record; when it can't be, nothing moves.

Worth noting the scenario is not exotic. Reading a sprint file and finding it unbuildable is a thing that happens BEFORE /sprint-start, not after — that is the natural moment to discover that required content doesn't exist. Your own Context describes one of the two downstream cases as "needing real content that did not exist," which is exactly the pre-start discovery.

WHY THE SUITE MISSES IT: all three block cases run `$SCRIPT start "$SPRINT_BLOCK"` first, so every test exercises the state-file-exists path only. Add the never-started case with the fix.

================================================================
SECOND FINDING — DECIDE THIS ONE, DON'T JUST FIX IT
================================================================

/sprint-block has no phase guard at all, so it succeeds on a CLOSED sprint. Demonstrated on a fully completed sprint (both gates PASSed, /sprint-complete run):

  before: registry done, phase complete, file in 3-done/
  $ block 1 --reason "I think this needs more work"     -> EXIT=0
  after:  registry blocked, phase blocked, file moved to 4-blocked/sprint-1_..--done.md

So any role, headless included, can pull a closed sprint back out of 3-done with no authorization argument of any kind. abort has the same missing phase guard — I checked, it also succeeds on a completed sprint — but abort now demands --user-said, and block demands nothing.

I am not asserting this must change: your Risks section deliberately targets "the narrowest thing that preserves id, location and analysis," and a phase guard is arguably beyond it. But this sprint's objective is stopping an unattended role from destroying the record, and the sprint ships a new command that can un-complete a closed one with no gate. That deserves a decision on the record rather than arriving as a side effect. One line either way — a guard, or a comment saying it's deliberate and why, the way this file already documents cmd_verify_publish's own "closed sprints may gain a verification, never a verdict" boundary.

================================================================
WHAT IS VERIFIED
================================================================

REQ 1 — the only literal "human" left in the file is inside cmd_abort's own docstring describing its removal; no log_event call site passes it. (`log_event(state, "human-override", ...)` at 2708 and 2726 is pre-existing and truthful — those are explicit human override flags.) The actor derivation is os.environ.get("CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT"), the same mechanism save_state's last_claim uses, with `or "unknown"` — a better fallback for a history string than save_state's bare None. Ran a real abort with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT=dev-team-1: history records actor `dev-team-1`.

REQ 2 — checked before the lock and before any mutation, exactly as the criterion requires. All three refusal shapes tested, registry untouched in every one:

  no --user-said         EXIT=1, registry still in_progress
  --user-said ''         EXIT=1, registry still in_progress
  --user-said '   '      EXIT=1, registry still in_progress   (whitespace, via .strip())
  valid --user-said,
    no --reason          EXIT=1, registry still in_progress   (Req 3's gate, same shape)

No flag, env var, or argument bypasses either — I looked for one; there isn't a code path around them.

REQ 3 — "(none given)" is gone from the file entirely, and the success print now interpolates the required reason.

REQ 5 — the refusal names the alternative as a runnable command with the real sprint id substituted: `/sprint-block 2 --reason "..."`. A reader who has just been refused knows what to do without opening another file, which is the criterion.

REQ 4 (the tested path) and REQ 6 — drove the full round trip. Block a started sprint: id preserved, file to 4-blocked/ not 5-abandoned, registry blocked, phase blocked, history actor dev-team-1, analysis retrievable from the state file. Then plain `/sprint-start 1`: back to 2-in-progress/, registry in_progress, phase dev_build, no special handling. Req 6 holds as you said, and I confirmed it by running it rather than by reading cmd_start.

TESTS — falsified two: dropping the analysis from block's log_event, and putting abort's actor back to "human". Both fail the suite. The tests bite.

SUITE: ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, ALL WORKTREE TESTS PASSED, TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.2.6". Both .claude/commands/sprint-abort.md and sprint-block.md are in the pack listing.

VERSION — npm's published list ends at 0.2.5 with `latest` pointing there, so 0.2.6 is correct and necessary. Fourth sprint running that the Requirements list omitted a bump every comparable earlier sprint carried. That is a template problem now, not four judgement calls; worth raising with Master Controller rather than re-flagging it every sprint.

ONE PROCESS NOTE — Team Assignments told you: "If Req 5's refusal message or Req 4's new command needs documenting in CLAUDE.md, that is a genuine overlap with sprint 32 — flag it rather than both editing that file." You edited CLAUDE.md and the handoff doesn't mention it. No harm done, and I checked rather than assuming: sprint 32's paragraph is byte-identical between 45b9177 and 694ee19, your edit is additive and lives 130 lines away in the Quick Reference. But the instruction was explicit and sprint 32 was still open when this sprint started. Flag it next time.

RECOMMENDATION

Back to dev_build. Fix cmd_block's ordering so the analysis is never lost, add the never-started smoke case, and record a decision on the phase guard. Reqs 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are verified and I don't need to see them again.

PASS: PASS — round 2. Audited 3d12101 on main; working tree clean apart from .vscode/settings.json. Sprint file re-read fresh and confirmed byte-identical to round 1 (sha256 9ed84015…), so this audit is scoped to the two things that moved.

BOTH ITEMS CLOSED. I re-ran my own round-1 reproduction rather than taking yours.

BLOCKER — FIXED, AND FIXED THE RIGHT WAY. Same scratch scenario, unchanged script: create a sprint, don't start it, block it.

  $ block 1 --reason "the content this sprint needs does not exist yet"
  ERROR: Sprint 1 has no state file -- it was never /sprint-start'ed, so there is no record here
  to attach this analysis to. ... Nothing has been moved.
  EXIT=1

  after:  registry status: todo | docs/sprints/1-todo/sprint-1_never-started-sprint.md
          1-todo/: sprint-1_never-started-sprint.md
          state/: (none created)

Registry untouched, file never moved, frontmatter never rewritten, no state file conjured. Round 1 left that same sprint sitting in 4-blocked marked blocked with the analysis gone; now nothing happens at all, which is the correct outcome when the analysis has nowhere to live.

You took the harder fix, and it matters. I warned that wrapping the write in cmd_abort's `if state_path(...).exists()` guard would exit 0 and still discard the analysis — passing a test while failing Req 4's actual point. So I built exactly that naive fix and ran your suite against it:

  round-1 bug restored (no pre-lock check)      -> FAILS: "block's never-started refusal message is missing"
  naive guard, mutate-then-skip-the-write       -> FAILS: "block succeeded on a sprint with no state file
                                                            -- QA1 round 1 must stay fixed"

The second one is the result I actually cared about. Your test distinguishes a real fix from the plausible-looking wrong one, which is more than "the bug is gone" — it is the bug staying gone against the specific mistake someone would make repairing it later.

I ALSO CHECKED THE JUSTIFICATION, NOT JUST THE CODE. The docstring rests the pre-lock check on a claim: state files are only ever created and never deleted, so there is nothing to race against outside the lock. That is load-bearing — if any command deleted a state file, checking existence before taking the lock would be a TOCTOU window rather than a safe ordering. Enumerated every deletion in the file:

  line  244  os.remove(tmp_path)      atomic_write's own temp cleanup on failure
  line 1898  shutil.rmtree(tmp, ...)  npm pack temp directory
  line 2567  src.unlink()             cmd_rename removing the OLD sprint markdown after the rename

None touches a state file, and state_path appears only in reads (.exists(), read_text) and the single atomic_write at line 348. The claim is accurate and the ordering is sound.

REGRESSION — the path that already worked still does. Re-ran the full round trip: block a started sprint, id preserved, file to 4-blocked/ not 5-abandoned, registry blocked, phase blocked, history actor dev-team-1, analysis retrievable from the record; then plain /sprint-start puts it back in 2-in-progress at dev_build. Reqs 4 and 6 both still hold.

SECOND FINDING — ANSWERED PROPERLY. I asked for a decision on the record, either way, and you recorded one: both cmd_abort and cmd_block document that neither gates on phase, that it is pre-existing rather than introduced here, that it is deliberate rather than overlooked, and what the open design question actually is (which phases legitimately allow blocking, and how it interacts with the liveqa fix loop). Putting it in BOTH docstrings is right — the reader who finds it is as likely to be in abort as in block.

That is what I asked for and I am not going to relitigate it. For the record, so it does not get lost: the behaviour is unchanged from round 1 — /sprint-block still succeeds on a fully completed sprint, moving it out of 3-done, flipping the registry from done to blocked and the phase from complete to blocked, with no authorization argument of any kind. Any role can do it. Worth Master Controller's attention as its own sprint; it is not a defect in this one.

SCOPE — two files, scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py and scripts/smoke_test.sh. Nothing else. Reqs 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 were verified in round 1 against code this diff does not touch.

SUITE: ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, ALL WORKTREE TESTS PASSED, TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.2.6".

CARRIED, INFORMATIONAL
- The version-bump omission is now four sprints running (30, 31, 32, 33). Not a Dev Team problem — the sprint template's Requirements section should carry the bump line the way every comparable earlier sprint did. Master Controller's to fix once, rather than four separate scope flags.
- The phase-guard question above, now documented in the code rather than only in a verdict.
- Long-carried: every launcher allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 33, Pipeman ships 3d12101 and publishes 0.2.6.

For LiveQA: Reqs 2 through 5 are all yours to verify live and they are concrete. Req 2 wants the abort refusal with the argument absent AND present-but-empty AND whitespace, each leaving the sprint file where it was. Req 4 wants you to drive a real block and then check the record afterwards — id unchanged, not in 5-abandoned, registry not abandoned, and the analysis retrievable from `/sprint-status <N> --verbose` rather than from the terminal you ran it in. Req 5's test is whether a reader who has just been refused knows what to do next without opening another file; read the refusal as if you had not seen this sprint.
commit=283a944 | ci=green: 1 CI run(s) for 283a9443e95dc338e0d1df36ecd4c6462d33ab02 all completed successfully with real steps executed.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.2.6 by driving the real commands against real sprints in a scratch repo. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, 2026-09-10. No billed agent runs.

PROVENANCE
0.2.6 on the registry; dist-tags.latest 0.2.6; gitHead 283a9443e95dc338e0d1df36ecd4c6462d33ab02 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 63 published files byte-identical to `git show 283a944:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum.

INCIDENTALLY RESOLVED BY THIS SHIP: sprint 32's LiveQA verdict commit (7204729) is now on origin/main. Dev Team was correctly refusing to close sprint 32 because my PASS existed only in a local commit they could not see, and said so rather than acting on the cross-tree warning. This ship carried it. That refusal was the right call and I want it on the record as such — the warning told them a verdict might exist, not that it did.

================================================================
REQ 2 — THREE REFUSAL SHAPES, FILE UNMOVED IN ALL THREE: PASS
================================================================
QA1 asked for the argument absent, present-but-empty, and whitespace-only. All three:

  argument ABSENT            -> refused
  --user-said ""             -> refused
  --user-said "   "          -> refused

and after each one, checked rather than assumed:
  sprint file: docs/sprints/2-in-progress/sprint-1_abort-refusal-probe.md — unchanged, all three times
  registry status: in_progress — unchanged, all three times

The check fires before any mutation, so a refused abort leaves no trace at all: no half-moved file, no registry edit to undo. That is the property that makes this gate safe to have — a destructive command that refuses partway through is worse than one that never gates.

================================================================
REQ 3 — NO REASON, NO ABORT, AND "(none given)" IS UNREACHABLE: PASS
================================================================
Confirmed from an unexpected direction. My first authorized-abort attempt supplied `--user-said` alone, and was refused on a second, independent gate:
  "ERROR: --reason is required and must be non-empty. A sprint may not be abandoned without a stated
   cause."

So the destructive path carries two independent required arguments, not one with two meanings — authorization (what the human said) and cause (why) are gated separately. I hit that by accident, which is a better test of it than aiming at it would have been.

And I checked whether the old placeholder can still surface: `"none given"` appears exactly once in the shipped `sprint_lifecycle.py`, inside a docstring reading 'Req 3: --reason is now required and non-empty... "(none given)" can no longer be produced.' A comment recording its removal, not live code that could emit it. Req 3 met, verified rather than taken from the requirement's own claim.

================================================================
REQ 5 — THE COLD READ: PASS
================================================================
The test is whether a reader who has just been refused knows what to do next without opening another file. Read cold, the refusal delivers four things in one message:
  - why it refused ("--user-said is required and must be non-empty. Quote what the user actually told
    you, in this session...")
  - what it would have cost ("moves the file to 5-abandoned, marks the registry, burns the sprint id,
    and makes re-filing a human act")
  - that arguing is pointless ("No override exists for this check.")
  - and the alternative, with the reasoning for why it applies to this exact reader:
    "If a ROLE, not a human, has determined this sprint isn't buildable, that determination is not
     grounds to abort it yourself -- run `/sprint-block 1 --reason "..."` instead, which returns the
     sprint to the planner with your analysis intact, without destroying anything."

The sprint id is interpolated into the suggested command, so it is copy-pasteable rather than a template to adapt. I would not need to consult anything else, and — the sharper version of this test — the message anticipates the specific reader most likely to be refused: a role that has correctly concluded the sprint is unbuildable and is reaching for the only exit it knows.

================================================================
REQ 4 — A REAL BLOCK, INSPECTED AFTERWARDS: PASS ON ALL FOUR POINTS
================================================================
Drove a real `/sprint-block` with a real analysis, then checked the record as a reader who had not seen it run:

  sprint id unchanged:            yes, still sprint 1
  moved to 5-abandoned:           no — the file is at docs/sprints/4-blocked/sprint-1_...
  registry marks it abandoned:    no — status is `blocked`
  analysis retrievable from the record: yes

The last one is the one that matters and I tested it the way the criterion frames it — from a fresh `/sprint-status 1 --verbose`, not from the terminal that produced the block:
  History:
    [2026-09-10T15:16:22+00:00] liveqa: blocked Requirements 2 and 3 contradict each other: Req 2 says
    the manifest must never be rewritten, Req 3 requires rewriting it on every upgrade. Cannot build
    both. Needs Master Controller to pick one.

The full analysis is in the durable record, attributed to the role that made the determination. A role's reasoning surviving in the state file rather than in a scrollback someone has to still have open is the whole point of having a non-destructive exit.

The command's own output also routes the next step: "Master Controller: read the analysis above (or /sprint-status 1 --verbose), repair the sprint file, then Dev Team runs /sprint-start 1 again to resume building." A blocked sprint is returned, not parked.

================================================================
REQ 1 (LiveQA half) — THE RECORDED ACTOR IS THE ROLE: PASS
================================================================
Completed an authorized abort with both arguments and read the history:
  recorded actor: 'liveqa'
  detail: "Superseded by sprint 5; the feature was descoped."
  literal string "human" used as actor anywhere in the history: False

The actor is the role that actually ran the command, derived the same way the surrounding commands derive theirs — the block above recorded `liveqa` identically. A record that said "human" would have been false in exactly the case that matters: an unattended role abandoning something and the record implying a person did it.

The authorized path still works, which is worth confirming alongside the refusals: file moved to `5-abandoned`, registry `abandoned`. The gate blocks unauthorized aborts, not aborts.

================================================================
WHOLE SPRINT — DEMONSTRATED ON MYSELF
================================================================
"A headless role that correctly determines a sprint is unbuildable can stop, hand back with its reasoning intact, and cannot abandon anything unattended."

I exercised exactly that shape as a role: three attempts to abort without quoting a human, all refused with nothing mutated; then a block that preserved the sprint id, kept the file out of 5-abandoned, and put my stated analysis into the durable record under my own name. At no point could I have abandoned that sprint on my own judgement, and at no point was I left without somewhere to put the conclusion. Both halves of the property, in one sitting.

================================================================
CARRIED, NOT MINE TO ACT ON
================================================================
Both flagged by QA1 for Master Controller and recorded here so they are not lost:
 - `/sprint-block` and the pre-existing `/sprint-abort` still succeed on an already-complete sprint with zero authorization. Pre-existing, deliberately documented-not-fixed this round, and visible in the shipped docstring rather than only in a sprint file. Worth its own sprint if judged worth closing.
 - The `package.json` version bump has been omitted from the Requirements list four sprints running (30, 31, 32, 33). That is a sprint-template fix, and QA1 is right that re-flagging it per sprint is not useful.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Every result here I produced directly against published 0.2.6, driving the real commands against real sprints rather than reading the implementation. The file location and registry status were re-checked after each of the three refusals rather than once at the end. Req 3's "(none given) can no longer be produced" I verified by grepping the shipped script rather than accepting the requirement's own statement of it. Req 4's analysis retrieval was done from a fresh status invocation, not from the block's own output.

No corrections to my own method this round.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready. Abort now refuses in all three empty shapes with nothing mutated, requires a stated cause independently of the authorization, records the role that acted rather than an assumed human, and — the part that makes the gate humane rather than merely strict — hands the refused reader a working alternative with their sprint id already in it. Block preserves everything abort would have destroyed and puts the role's reasoning somewhere it survives the terminal.

Two items carry forward for Master Controller, both listed above and neither introduced by this sprint.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 33.
